summary: Describes an abstract mechanism by which senders tell the network about congestion recently experienced by packets in their flow, so network elements can see the congestion as well as the receiver.

why do senders need to report congestion
subtitle: Letting the network see what congestion senders have caused

tldr.problem: Today, only the receiver learns about network congestion through packet loss or ECN marks and feeds this back to the sender, but the network itself does not see the full picture of congestion a sender is causing throughout the path.
tldr.mechanism: Congestion Exposure (ConEx) enables senders to reflect congestion information back into the network at the IP layer, so network devices along the path can see which flows are causing congestion and apply traffic management policies.
tldr.outcome: Networks can better manage congestion by targeting policies at flows that cause congestion rather than guessing based on bit rates, and the visibility creates incentives for applications to share the network more fairly.

facts.label: Requires
facts.value: Modified senders; optional receiver and forwarding changes

today: RFC 7713 is an Informational document that defines the abstract mechanism and requirements for ConEx. Concrete implementations have been developed in IPv6 (ConEx Destination Option) and IPv4. ConEx remains largely deployed in research and some data center networks but has not achieved widespread Internet deployment. The mechanisms and audit approaches described here remain relevant for traffic management research and experimentation.

sections.title: The Congestion Information Gap
sections.content:
Congestion Exposure (ConEx) is a mechanism for senders to relay information about network congestion back through the network itself. Today, when a network device (a router or switch) detects congestion, it signals the receiver by dropping packets or marking them with Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN). The receiver passes this information back to the sender through transport-layer feedback, and the sender adjusts its sending rate. However, the intermediate network devices that caused the congestion never learn what the sender did in response.

This document describes an abstract mechanism by which senders can tell the network, in-band at the IP layer, about congestion they have experienced. This visibility allows network devices along the path to implement traffic management policies based on actual congestion caused by each flow, rather than guessing based on throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices today can see that there is congestion, but they do not know if senders have slowed down to help fix it. ConEx lets senders tell the network that they experienced congestion and slowed down, so the network can see that the problem is being handled.

sections.title: How ConEx Signals Flow Through the Network
sections.content:
The RFC describes the flow of congestion information as a cycle. A congested network device sends a congestion signal (loss or ECN mark) to the receiver. The receiver feeds this back to the sender through acknowledgments or other feedback mechanisms. The sender then re-echoes this information in new packets sent forward through the network, where policy devices along the path can observe it and act on it.

The abstract mechanism defines several types of ConEx signals: Re-Echo-Loss indicates the sender experienced packet loss; Re-Echo-ECN indicates ECN marking; Credit indicates the sender is building up advance notice of potential future congestion; and ConEx-Not-Marked indicates the transport is ConEx-capable but not signaling any of the above. The document emphasizes that this is abstract—specific bit encodings and codepoints are left to concrete protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The congestion information flows in a circle: the network tells the receiver about congestion, the receiver tells the sender, and the sender tells the network that it knows about the congestion. Policy devices look at these messages from senders to decide how to manage traffic.

sections.title: Signals, Encoding, and Audit Requirements
sections.content:
ConEx Signals must be visible to network devices at the IP layer, remain unchanged once set by the sender, and work under partial deployment. The mechanism should encourage deployment of ECN but not require it. Several encoding approaches are presented: a naive encoding (simple bit marking, not auditable), a null encoding (inferring congestion from TCP headers), an ECN-based encoding (similar to re-ECN), independent bits (separate flags for each signal type), and codepoint encodings (mutually exclusive signal values).

A critical requirement is auditability. Without audit, senders have incentive to understate the congestion they cause to avoid policy penalties. The audit function must count ConEx Signals to verify they represent actual congestion, using techniques like ECN auditing (comparing ECN marks with ConEx signals), TCP-specific loss auditing, or predominant bottleneck loss auditing. The unit of congestion (bytes vs. packets) must be explicitly specified in any concrete encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The network needs to be able to check that senders are not lying about congestion, otherwise senders would claim they did not cause any problems even when they did. The audit function watches for dishonest senders and applies penalties if they cheat.

sections.title: Protocol Components: Senders, Policy, and Audit
sections.content:
ConEx requires modified senders that monitor feedback and send ConEx signals. Unmodified receivers can generally work with ConEx senders (except in the case of TCP with ECN, where more precise feedback is beneficial). Policy devices can be deployed at network borders to monitor ConEx Signals and enforce congestion-based policies: congestion monitoring devices track signals to compare against policy, and congestion policers limit traffic from flows causing excessive congestion downstream.

A key design goal is that important policy mechanisms should not require per-flow state in the core network. Instead, policies can operate on aggregates of traffic, tracking the total congestion caused by a user, site, or type of traffic. Audit devices may require per-flow state at the edges where traffic is less aggregated, but they enable policy elsewhere without that burden. The audit function prevents widespread cheating by applying sanctions (throttling, dropping packets) against flows that understate congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: Senders need to be updated to send ConEx signals. The network can have devices that watch for congestion and slow down traffic from flows that cause problems. These devices check that senders are telling the truth about congestion, and punish those who lie by slowing them down.

sections.title: Incentives for Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
ConEx is designed to work under partial deployment. Packets can indicate whether they use ConEx on a per-packet basis. Senders can deploy ConEx independently; receivers need not be modified (except for TCP-ECN feedback precision); forwarding need not change; and network policy devices can be deployed unilaterally at network borders to monitor ConEx on incoming traffic. Networks can create incentives for ConEx adoption by offering better treatment to ConEx-capable traffic or by allowing ConEx sources greater freedom while treating non-ConEx traffic more conservatively.

An operator can audit ConEx at network edges unilaterally without coordinating with other networks. If ConEx is understated in traffic entering a downstream network, that network can detect it and apply penalties. This independence allows each network to protect itself without requiring end-to-end coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every sender, router, or network needs to use ConEx at the same time. Some senders can start using it, some networks can start checking for it, and the system still works because each part can work with both ConEx and non-ConEx traffic.

sections.title: Security, Attacks, and Audit Defense
sections.content:
The primary security concern is that users and applications have strong motivation to understate congestion to avoid policy penalties. ConEx cannot prevent this incentive, but audit mechanisms can make cheating unprofitable. Attacks include flow ID whitewashing (starting new flows after being caught cheating), dragging down aggregates (mixing bad flows with good ones), identity spoofing, dummy traffic, and signal poisoning.

The audit function must have minimal false hits (penalizing honest flows), quickly detect and sanction dishonest flows, be transport-oblivious (not assuming specific congestion control algorithms), apply sufficient and proportionate penalties, manage memory exhaustion attacks, and prevent identity whitewashing. The document notes that more detailed security analysis should accompany concrete protocol specifications, referring readers to research on re-ECN audit techniques as a starting point.
sections.plainLanguage: People will try to cheat by not reporting congestion they caused. The audit function has to catch cheaters and punish them fairly so they do not gain anything from lying, but without being so strict that it penalizes honest people.
